sentences.t: Hrōðgār maþelode, helm Scyldinga:
sentences.l: Hrothgar spoke in speech-words, helm of the Scyldings:
sentences.i: Hrothgar spoke in formal words, protector of the Scyldings:
sentences.n: The same introduction as at 371 and 456, with the house renderings: ‘maþelode’ is the past of ‘maþelian’, the verb that opens a formal speech, and ‘helm Scyldinga’ is ‘helm (protector) of the Scyldings’, in apposition to the name. The colon opens a long speech. It answers the question that closed the last part, whether the night had been a comfortable one.

sentences.t: ‘Ne frīn þū æfter sǣlum!
sentences.l: ‘Not ask you after joys!
sentences.i: ‘Do not ask after happiness!
sentences.n: ‘Ne frīn’ is a negative command: ‘ne’ with the imperative of ‘frignan’ (‘fregnan’), ‘ask’, so ‘do not ask’. ‘æfter sǣlum’ is ‘after joys’; ‘sǣlum’ is the dative plural of ‘sǣl’, ‘happiness, good fortune, good time’, and ‘æfter’ with ‘frignan’ means ‘ask about’. The opening quotation mark is Klaeber’s, as printed in ‘t’. Hrothgar brushes aside Beowulf’s courteous inquiry about the night.

sentences.t:
Sorh is genīwod
Denigea lēodum.
sentences.l: Sorrow is renewed to the Danes’ people.
sentences.i: Sorrow is made new again for the Danish people.
sentences.n: ‘Sorh is genīwod’ is ‘sorrow is renewed’: ‘genīwod’ is the past participle of ‘genīwian’, ‘renew’. ‘Denigea’ is the genitive plural of ‘Denige’, a longer form of the people-name ‘Dene’ (the Danes), with ‘lēodum’ the dative plural, ‘to the people’. What the sorrow is comes in the next unit.

sentences.t:
Dēad is Æschere,
Yrmenlāfes yldra brōþor,
mīn rūnwita ond mīn rǣdbora,
eaxlgestealla, ðonne wē on orlege
hafelan weredon, þonne hniton fēþan,
eoferas cnysedan.
sentences.l: Dead is Æschere, Yrmenlaf’s elder brother, my rune-knower and my counsel-bearer, shoulder-companion, when we in war our heads guarded, when the footmen clashed, boars crushed.
sentences.i: Æschere is dead, Yrmenlaf’s elder brother, my confidant and my counsellor, my comrade at the shoulder, when in war we guarded our heads, when the foot-troops clashed and the boar-crests were crushed.
sentences.n: ‘Dēad is Æschere’ puts the news before the name. ‘Yrmenlāfes’ is genitive, ‘yldra brōþor’ ‘elder brother’; the brother is named only here, as far as I can tell. The next three nouns are nominatives in apposition to Æschere, each a compound: ‘rūnwita’ (‘rūn’, secret or counsel, + ‘wita’, one who knows), ‘rǣdbora’ (‘rǣd’, counsel, + ‘bora’, bearer, one who carries advice), and ‘eaxlgestealla’ (‘eaxl’ shoulder + ‘gestealla’ comrade, one who stood at one’s shoulder). The two ‘ðonne/þonne’ clauses (‘when’) say when: ‘on orlege’ is ‘in war’ (dative), ‘hafelan weredon’ is ‘guarded heads’ (‘wē’, we, is the subject, Hrothgar and Æschere together), and ‘hniton fēþan’ is ‘foot-troops clashed’, ‘hniton’ being the past plural of ‘hnītan’, ‘clash’, and ‘fēþan’ a collective for infantry (a plural I take as the subject). ‘eoferas cnysedan’ has no conjunction (it is on line 1328). ‘eoferas’ is ‘boars’; helmets carried a boar image (compare ‘Eoforlīc’ at 303), so ‘boars’ stands for boar-crested helmets, a kenning I am inferring from that. ‘cnysedan’ is the past plural of ‘cnyssan’, ‘strike, crush’. The grammar does not settle the roles: ‘eoferas’ could be the subject (‘the boars crashed’) or the object (‘[they] crushed the boars’), because the nominative and accusative plural are the same. The idiomatic version takes it as the object, ‘the boar-crests were crushed’; the clause does not say whose helmets they were.

sentences.t:
Swy(lc) scolde eorl wesan,
[æþeling] ǣrgōd, swylc Æschere wæs!
sentences.l: Such should a man be, an atheling good-from-of-old, such as Æschere was!
sentences.i: That is what a warrior should be, a prince of old-proven goodness, such as Æschere was!
sentences.n: ‘Swylc … swylc’ means ‘such … as’. The parentheses in ‘Swy(lc)’ are Klaeber’s: the apparatus gives the reading at folio 159b as ‘swy . . scolde’ (from transcript B, with A), the rest being lost, and Thorkelin’s edition prints ‘swylc’. The brackets in ‘[æþeling]’ mean the whole word is supplied: Grundtvig proposed ‘ædeling’, Grein the spelling ‘æðeling’, and it is a guess, though one that fits the sense and the ‘æþeling ǣrgōd’ of line 130 in the second fitt. ‘scolde … wesan’ is ‘should be’ (the past of ‘sculan’ with the infinitive), and ‘eorl’ is ‘man, warrior’. ‘ǣrgōd’ is ‘good from of old’ (‘ǣr’, before, + ‘gōd’), the word the published parts render ‘good-from-of-old’ at 130 and ‘good of old’ at 989; ‘old-proven’ is my idiomatic reading and the exact sense is a guess.

sentences.t:
Wearð him on Heorote tō handbanan
wælgǣst wǣfre;
sentences.l: Became to him in Heorot as hand-slayer a slaughter-ghost wandering;
sentences.i: In Heorot a roaming slaughter-spirit became his slayer;
sentences.n: ‘Wearð’ is ‘became’, and ‘tō handbanan’ is ‘as hand-slayer’ (dative singular after ‘tō’): ‘bana’ is ‘slayer’, ‘hand’ the means, so one who kills with the hand, and ‘him’ is Æschere, a dative of the person affected. The subject is ‘wælgǣst wǣfre’, ‘wæl’ (slaughter, the slain) + ‘gǣst’ (spirit), a ‘slaughter-ghost’, here Grendel’s mother, though Hrothgar does not call her ‘she’ until the next sentence. ‘wǣfre’ is an adjective, ‘wavering, restless, wandering’, from the lexica; I read it as ‘roaming’. Klaeber ends the unit with a semicolon.

sentences.t:
ic ne wāt hwæder
atol ǣse wlanc eftsīðas tēah,
fylle gefægnod.
sentences.l: I do not know whither the terrible one, proud of carrion, its return-journeys drew, by its fill made glad.
sentences.i: I do not know where that terrible creature, exulting in its carrion, took its way back, glad of its fill.
sentences.n: ‘ic ne wāt’ is ‘I do not know’ (‘wāt’, first person singular present of ‘witan’). ‘hwæder’ is ‘whither’, and the italic ‘d’ is Klaeber’s change: the manuscript has ‘hwæþer’ (‘whether’); Grein in his first edition (with a query), Sweet and others read ‘hwider’, ‘whither’, and Heyne (first edition) and Holthausen keep ‘hwæþer’ but take it to mean ‘whither’ (apparatus). The subject is two adjectives used as nouns, ‘atol … wlanc’, ‘terrible, proud’: ‘ǣse’ is the dative of ‘ǣs’, ‘carrion, food’ (my reading from the lexica), and it says what the creature was proud of, the corpse. ‘eftsīðas tēah’ is ‘drew (took) return-journeys’, ‘tēah’ the past of ‘tēon’, ‘draw, go’. ‘fylle gefægnod’ is ‘by (her) fill made glad’: ‘fylle’ is the dative of ‘fyllu’, ‘fullness, a meal’, ‘gefægnod’ the past participle of ‘gefægnian’, ‘gladden’. The manuscript has ‘ge frægnod’ (‘ge’ and ‘frægnod’ as two words), and Klaeber and most editors read ‘gefægnod’, compare ‘fylle gefēan’ at 562 and ‘fylle gefǣgon’ at 1014, where ‘fill’ goes with a word of rejoicing; two editors (‘Tho.’ and ‘Tr.’ in the apparatus) read ‘gefrēfrod’, ‘comforted’, and Grundtvig ‘gefrecnod’. The adjectives do not show whether the creature is ‘he’ or ‘she’, so both versions say ‘it’; the next sentence supplies ‘Hēo’.

sentences.t:
Hēo þā fǣhðe wræc,
þē þū gystran niht Grendel cwealdest
þurh hǣstne hād heardum clammum,
forþan hē tō lange lēode mīne
wanode ond wyrde.
sentences.l: She that feud avenged, that you last night Grendel killed through a violent condition with hard clamps, because he too long my people lessened and ruined.
sentences.i: She has avenged that feud, the one in which last night you killed Grendel by violent means, with hard grips, because for too long he had lessened and ruined my people.
sentences.n: ‘Hēo’ is ‘she’, the first time Hrothgar says it. ‘wræc’ is the past of ‘wrecan’, ‘avenge, drive’, with ‘þā fǣhðe’ (‘that feud’, ‘þā’ the accusative feminine of the demonstrative) as the object; ‘þē’ then introduces a relative clause (‘which’) saying what the feud was: ‘þū gystran niht Grendel cwealdest’, ‘you killed Grendel last night’ (‘gystran niht’ is an accusative of time, ‘yester-night’). ‘þurh hǣstne hād’ is a crux in meaning: ‘hǣstne’ is the accusative of the adjective ‘hǣst’, ‘violent’ (the same word as the noun ‘hǣst’, violence), and ‘hād’ is ‘person, state, manner’, so ‘by a violent manner’, or ‘by a violent person’; I render ‘violent condition’ in the literal version and ‘violent means’ in the idiomatic one, both guesses. ‘heardum clammum’ is the dative plural ‘with hard clamps’ (‘clamm’, bond, grip), Beowulf’s hand-hold. ‘forþan … wanode ond wyrde’ gives the reason: Grendel ‘lessened’ (‘wanode’, from ‘wanian’) and ‘ruined’ (‘wyrde’, from ‘wyrdan’) Hrothgar’s people ‘tō lange’, too long.

sentences.t:
Hē æt wīge gecrang
ealdres scyldig, ond nū ōþer cwōm
mihtig mānscaða, wolde hyre mǣg wrecan,
gē feor hafað fǣhðe gestǣled,
þæs þe þincean mæg þegne monegum,
sē þe æfter sincgyfan on sefan grēoteþ, —
sentences.l: He at battle fell, of life guilty, and now another came, a mighty crime-scather, would her kinsman avenge, and far has the feud established, as it may seem to many a thane, he who for the treasure-giver in his mind weeps, —
sentences.i: He fell in the fight, forfeit of his life, and now another has come, a mighty wicked marauder, who wanted to avenge her kinsman, and she has carried the feud far, as it may seem to many a thane, one who mourns in his heart for the treasure-giver, —
sentences.n: ‘Hē’ is Grendel. ‘ealdres scyldig’ is ‘guilty of (owing) his life’: ‘ealdres’ is genitive, so he was forfeit, his life owed. ‘ōþer’ is ‘another’; ‘mānscaða’ is the house ‘crime-scather’ (rendered ‘wicked marauder’ at 712), grammatically masculine though the creature is a mother. ‘wolde hyre mǣg wrecan’ is ‘wanted to avenge her kinsman’ (‘mǣg’, kinsman, here her son Grendel). ‘gē feor hafað fǣhðe gestǣled’ is the hard clause: ‘gē’ I take as ‘and’ (it can also mean ‘also’), ‘feor’ ‘far’, ‘hafað … gestǣled’ ‘has … established’, but ‘gestǣled’ looks like the past participle of a verb ‘stǣlan’ (perhaps ‘set up, establish’) that I cannot pin down from the lexica, so ‘carried the feud far’ is inferred from the sense, a guess. ‘þæs þe þincean mæg þegne monegum’ is ‘as it may seem to many a thane’ (‘þincean’ is the infinitive of ‘þyncan’, ‘seem’, ‘þegne monegum’ a dative). ‘sē þe … grēoteþ’ is ‘he who weeps’, and ‘sē’ is nominative, not the dative that would follow ‘þegne monegum’, so the clause hangs loose; the literal version says ‘he’ and the idiomatic one ‘one who’. ‘sincgyfan’ is ‘treasure-giver’ (as at 1012). The text does not say who mourns or who the treasure-giver is. Klaeber ends with a dash because the sentence breaks off.

sentences.t: hreþerbealo hearde;
sentences.l: breast-bale, hard;
sentences.i: a bitter grief in the heart;
sentences.n: The sentence resumes after the dash: ‘hreþerbealo’ is ‘hreþer’ (breast, heart, mind) + ‘bealo’ (evil, harm, woe), a ‘breast-bale’, and ‘hearde’ most likely an adverb, ‘hard, sorely’ (a strong neuter adjective in the nominative would have no ending). I read it as an exclamation without a verb: ‘a breast-bale, sorely [felt]’; it could also be taken as the object of ‘grēoteþ’ before the dash (‘weeps a breast-bale’).

sentences.t:
nū sēo hand ligeð,
sē þe ēow wēlhwylcra wilna dohte.
sentences.l: now the hand lies, that to you of nearly every wish availed.
sentences.i: Now the hand lies still that served you in nearly every wish.
sentences.n: ‘sēo hand’ is a feminine noun, ‘the hand’, meaning Æschere’s hand (and so the man); ‘ligeð’ is ‘lies’. ‘sē þe’ is masculine ‘who’, which does not agree with ‘hand’, and some editors (apparatus) read ‘sē[o]’, with a feminine ending, which is how they bring the relative into agreement; the sense is the same either way. ‘ēow … dohte’ is ‘availed you’: ‘dugan’ takes the dative of the person, here the plural ‘ēow’ (you Danes), and the genitive of the thing, ‘wēlhwylcra wilna’ (‘of nearly every wish’, both genitive plural).

sentences.t:
Ic þæt londbūend, lēode mīne,
selerǣdende secgan hȳrde,
þæt hīe gesāwon swylce twēgen
micle mearcstapan mōras healdan,
ellorgǣstas.
sentences.l: I that land-dwellers, my people, hall-counsellors, say heard, that they saw such two great mark-steppers moors hold, elsewhere-ghosts.
sentences.i: I have heard my people, the dwellers in the land, the counsellors of the hall, say this: that they have seen two such great stalkers of the borderlands holding the moors, spirits from elsewhere.
sentences.n: ‘Ic þæt … secgan hȳrde’ is ‘I heard say that’; ‘þæt’ is the object (this), anticipating the ‘þæt’ clause that follows. ‘londbūend’ and ‘selerǣdende’ are accusative plurals, the objects of ‘hȳrde’ (‘I heard land-dwellers … say’): ‘londbūend’ is ‘land-dwellers’ (‘bū-’, dwell), ‘lēode mīne’ ‘my people’ in apposition, and ‘selerǣdende’ ‘hall-counsellors’ (‘sele’, hall, + ‘rǣdend’, one who advises or rules), whose exact sense is guessed. ‘hīe gesāwon’ is ‘they saw’, and ‘swylce twēgen’ ‘two such’ (‘swylce’ could also be ‘likewise’). ‘mearcstapan’ is the plural of ‘mearcstapa’, ‘mark-stepper’, the epithet of Grendel at 103. ‘mōras healdan’ is ‘hold the moors’ (infinitive after ‘gesāwon’). ‘ellorgǣstas’ is ‘elsewhere-ghosts’ (‘ellor’, elsewhere, + ‘gǣst’), spirits from somewhere else, as at 807.

sentences.l: Of those the one was, as they most certainly could discern, a woman’s likeness;
sentences.i: One of the two was, as far as they could make out for certain, in the likeness of a woman;
sentences.n: ‘Ðǣra ōðer’ is ‘of those, the one’ (‘ðǣra’ a genitive plural). ‘þæs þe hīe gewislīcost gewitan meahton’ is ‘as they could most certainly discern’ (‘gewislīcost’ a superlative adverb, ‘gewitan’ an infinitive, ‘know’, ‘meahton’ ‘could’). ‘idese onlīcnes’ is ‘a woman’s likeness’: ‘idese’ is a genitive singular of ‘ides’, ‘woman’, and ‘onlīcnes’ a nominative noun, ‘likeness’. This is an editors’ form: the manuscript has two words, ‘onlic næs’, and Kemble and most editors join them to ‘onlīcnes’; Grundtvig, Sweet and Holthausen read ‘onlīc’ (an adjective, ‘like’), Sweet adding ‘wæs’ before the next ‘ōðer’, which opens the next unit. The italic ‘es’ is the change.

sentences.l: the other, wretchedly shaped, in a man’s form exile-tracks trod, except he was greater than any other man;
sentences.i: the other, a wretchedly shaped thing, in the form of a man, trod the tracks of an exile, except that he was bigger than any other man;
sentences.n: ‘ōðer earmsceapen’ is ‘the other, wretched-shaped’ (‘earm’, wretched, + ‘sceapen’, shaped). ‘on weres wæstmum’ is ‘in a man’s form’: ‘weres’ genitive, ‘wæstmum’ dative plural of ‘wæstm’, ‘growth, shape’. ‘wræclāstas træd’ is ‘trod exile-tracks’ (‘wræc’, exile, + ‘lāst’, track, the accusative plural object of ‘træd’, past of ‘tredan’), a phrase for the path of one driven out. ‘næfne’ is ‘except that, unless’, and ‘māra þonne ǣnig man ōðer’ is ‘greater than any other man’, the comparative with ‘þonne’. The pronoun ‘hē’ is masculine, so the second creature is male.

sentences.t:
þone on gēardagum Grendel nemdon
foldbūende;
sentences.l: whom in days-of-yore Grendel named earth-dwellers;
sentences.i: him the dwellers on the earth called Grendel in days gone by;
sentences.n: ‘þone’ is the accusative of the demonstrative, ‘whom’ in the literal version and ‘him’ in the idiomatic one, pointing to the second of the pair just described; the verb comes before its subject, so ‘Grendel nemdon … foldbūende’ is ‘named Grendel … earth-dwellers’. ‘gēardagum’ is ‘in days of yore’ (‘gēar’, year, + ‘dagum’, days, dative plural). ‘foldbūende’ is the plural subject ‘earth-dwellers’ (‘fold’, earth, + ‘būend’, dweller), as the ‘londbūend’ of 1345. The last letter of ‘nemdon’ is italic: the manuscript has ‘nemdod’ and Kemble set it right (apparatus).

sentences.t:
nō hīe fæder cunnon,
hwæþer him ǣnig wæs ǣr ācenned
dyrnra gāsta.
sentences.l: not they a father know, whether to him any was before begotten of hidden spirits.
sentences.i: They know no father, and do not know whether any of the hidden spirits was born to him in earlier time.
sentences.n: ‘nō hīe fæder cunnon’ is ‘they do not know a father’ (‘cunnon’ the plural of ‘cunnan’, ‘know’). The ‘hwæþer’ clause says what they do not know: ‘whether any of the hidden spirits had been begotten (‘ācenned’) before to him’, with ‘him’ a dative of possession and ‘dyrnra gāsta’ a genitive plural, ‘of the hidden spirits’ (‘dyrne’, hidden, secret). The sense is that no one knows if he had a father among the spirits. The word is ‘hwæþer’ here as the manuscript has it, where at 1331 Klaeber changed it to ‘hwæder’.

sentences.t:
Hīe dȳgel lond
warigeað wulfhleoþu, windige næssas,
frēcne fengelād, ðǣr fyrgenstrēam
under næssa genipu niþer gewīteð,
flōd under foldan.
sentences.l: They secret land ward, wolf-slopes, windy headlands, perilous fen-path, where mountain-stream under the headlands’ mists downward departs, flood under the earth.
sentences.i: They inhabit a hidden land, wolf-haunted slopes, windy headlands, a dangerous fen-path, where the mountain stream goes down under the mists of the headlands, a flood under the earth.
sentences.n: ‘Hīe’ is the two creatures. ‘warigeað’ is the plural of ‘warian’, ‘guard, inhabit’, the verb of 1253 in the last part, so ‘ward’ in the literal. ‘dȳgel lond’ is ‘secret land’, and the objects that follow are in apposition. ‘wulfhleoþu’ is ‘wolf-slopes’ (‘wulf’ + ‘hleoþ’, slope, cliff, a plural noun), ‘windige næssas’ ‘windy headlands’ (‘næss’, headland), ‘frēcne fengelād’ ‘perilous fen-path’. ‘fengelād’ is a rare word and ‘fen-path’ (‘fenn’ + ‘gelād’, way, passage) is a guess at its first part. ‘ðǣr fyrgenstrēam’ introduces the relative clause: ‘fyrgen’ means ‘mountain’, so ‘mountain-stream’, a word that occurs rarely and may carry other senses. ‘under næssa genipu’ is ‘under the headlands’ mists’ (‘genipu’ a plural noun, ‘mists, darkness’), ‘niþer gewīteð’ ‘goes down’, and ‘flōd under foldan’ ‘a flood under earth’, an apposition describing the stream.

sentences.t:
Nis þæt feor heonon
mīlgemearces, þæt se mere standeð;
sentences.l: Not-is that far from here of mile-measure, that the mere stands;
sentences.i: It is not far from here, measured in miles, to where the mere stands;
sentences.n: ‘Nis’ is ‘ne is’, ‘is not’; ‘mīlgemearces’ is a genitive of measure, ‘in mile-marking’, so ‘by the measure of a mile’; and ‘þæt’ opens a clause saying where: ‘that the mere stands’. ‘mere’ here is a lake or pool (the Modern English ‘mere’), not the sea, which the same word meant in ‘merelīðende’ at 255. The ‘d’ of ‘standeð’ is italic because the manuscript reads ‘stanðeð’, which Thorkelin set right (apparatus). The semicolon is Klaeber’s.

sentences.t:
ofer þǣm hongiað hrinde bearwas,
wudu wyrtum fæst wæter oferhelmað.
sentences.l: over it hang bark-covered groves, wood fast by its roots overshadows the water.
sentences.i: Over it hang bark-clad groves; the firmly rooted wood overshadows the water.
sentences.n: ‘ofer þǣm’ is ‘over it’ (the mere). ‘hrinde’ is disputed. Klaeber prints ‘hrinde’ (after Wright; Klaeber refers to his Glossary); I take it as an adjective from ‘hrind’, ‘bark, rind’, ‘covered with bark’; other editors read ‘hrīmge’, ‘frosty’ (Morris, Sweet), ‘hrīmde’, ‘frosted’ (Cosijn), or ‘hringde’, ‘ringed’ (Sedgefield). I follow ‘bark-covered’ as a guess among these. ‘wudu wyrtum fæst’ is ‘wood fast by roots’, ‘wyrtum’ a dative plural of ‘wyrt’, ‘root, plant’. ‘oferhelmað’ is ‘overshadows, covers over’ (from ‘helm’, a covering, and ‘ofer’), its object ‘wæter’, Its subject is the singular ‘wudu’, ‘wood’, not the plural ‘bearwas’; ‘wudu’ and ‘wæter’ are both neuter, so the form does not tell subject from object, and the singular verb and the sense decide it.

sentences.t:
Þǣr mæg nihta gehwǣm nīðwundor sēon,
fȳr on flōde.
sentences.l: There may each of nights a malice-wonder be seen, fire on the flood.
sentences.i: There every night one may see a dreadful wonder, fire on the water.
sentences.n: ‘mæg … sēon’ is ‘may see’, with no subject stated (‘one’). ‘nihta gehwǣm’ is ‘each night’, a dative of time with ‘gehwǣm’ ‘each’ and ‘nihta’ the partitive genitive plural. ‘nīðwundor’ is ‘nīð’ (enmity, malice, affliction) + ‘wundor’ (wonder), a ‘dread wonder’; I find the compound only in this line, so ‘malice-wonder’ in the literal is my construction and ‘dreadful wonder’ a guess. ‘fȳr on flōde’, ‘fire on the flood’, is in apposition to it.

sentences.t:
Nō þæs frōd leofað
gumena bearna, þæt þone grund wite.
sentences.l: None so wise lives of the children of men, that he the bottom knows.
sentences.i: No one among the children of men lives who is wise enough to know its bottom.
sentences.n: ‘Nō þæs frōd leofað … þæt …’ is ‘none lives so wise that …’: ‘þæs’ with ‘frōd’ is ‘so wise’, and the ‘þæt’ clause with the subjunctive ‘wite’ (‘may know’) gives the result. ‘gumena bearna’ is a partitive genitive plural, ‘of the children of men’, so ‘none of the children of men lives so wise’. ‘grund’ is ‘bottom’ (of the mere).

sentences.t:
Ðēah þe hǣðstapa hundum geswenced,
heorot hornum trum holtwudu sēce,
feorran geflȳmed, ǣr hē feorh seleð,
aldor on ōfre, ǣr hē in wille,
hafelan [beorgan];
sentences.l: Though the heath-stepper, by hounds harassed, a hart strong in horns, a forest seek, driven from afar, sooner he gives up life, his lifetime on the bank, than he go in, to save his head;
sentences.i: Even if the stag that ranges the heath, strong in his antlers, hard pressed by hounds and driven from far off, makes for the wood, he will give up his life on the bank sooner than choose to go in to save his head;
sentences.n: ‘Ðēah þe’ is ‘though’ and takes the subjunctive ‘sēce’ (‘seek’). The subject is ‘hǣðstapa’, ‘heath-stepper’ (‘hǣð’, heath, + ‘stapa’, stepper), a name for the stag, in apposition to ‘heorot hornum trum’, ‘a hart strong in horns’. ‘hundum geswenced’ is ‘harassed by hounds’ (‘swencan’), ‘feorran geflȳmed’ ‘driven from afar’, ‘holtwudu’ ‘wood, forest’. Then ‘ǣr … ǣr’ is ‘sooner … than’: ‘ǣr hē feorh seleð, aldor on ōfre’ is ‘sooner he gives up life, breath on the bank’ (‘aldor’ is ‘life’ in apposition to ‘feorh’, ‘ōfre’ the dative of ‘ōfer’, ‘bank’), and ‘ǣr hē in wille’ is ‘than he will (go) in’, the verb of motion omitted. The ending is a crux. The manuscript has ‘hafelan :’ with no verb, and Klaeber’s ‘[beorgan]’ is Holthausen’s suggestion, marked with a query, ‘save’; Kemble and most editors read ‘[hȳdan]’, ‘hide’. The sense, ‘to save (hide) his head’, is the same either way, but the word is a guess.

sentences.t: nis þæt hēoru stōw!
sentences.l: not-is that a pleasant place!
sentences.i: That is no pleasant place!
sentences.n: ‘nis’ is ‘ne is’, ‘is not’. ‘hēoru’ is a feminine nominative agreeing with ‘stōw’, ‘place’, and I take it as the adjective ‘hēore’, ‘gentle, pleasant, safe’; ‘pleasant’ is a guess from the lexica, since the word is rare. The litotes (the understatement for ‘it is a terrible place’) closes the first half of the description of the mere.

sentences.t:
Þonon ȳðgeblond ūp āstīgeð
won tō wolcnum, þonne wind styreþ
lāð gewidru, oð þæt lyft drysmaþ,
roderas rēotað.
sentences.l: Thence wave-blending up ascends dark to the clouds, when wind stirs hateful weathers, until the air darkens, the heavens weep.
sentences.i: From it a surging of waves climbs up, dark, to the clouds, when the wind stirs up hateful storms, until the air grows dim and the skies weep.
sentences.n: ‘Þonon’ is ‘from there’. ‘ȳðgeblond’ is ‘ȳð’ (wave) + ‘geblond’ (a mixing, from ‘blandan’), a ‘wave-blending’, the churning of the water. ‘won’ is ‘dark’ and ‘tō wolcnum’ ‘to the clouds’. ‘þonne wind styreþ lāð gewidru’ is ‘when wind stirs hateful weathers’; ‘gewidru’ is a plural noun for storms, ‘lāð’ ‘hateful’. ‘oð þæt’ is ‘until’. ‘drysmaþ’ is ‘grows dark, gloomy’, from a verb I find only here, and the sense is guessed from the context. ‘roderas rēotað’ is ‘the heavens weep’: ‘roderas’ is the nominative plural of ‘rodor’, ‘sky’, and ‘rēotað’ the plural of ‘rēotan’, ‘weep, lament’; the weeping is presumably rain. ‘drysmaþ’ is the doubtful word, and ‘the heavens weep’ is a figure that I take to mean rain, so I give the clause as a guess.

sentences.t:
Nū is se rǣd gelang
eft æt þē ānum.
sentences.l: Now is the counsel dependent again on you alone.
sentences.i: Now once more what is to be done depends on you alone.
sentences.n: ‘Nū is se rǣd gelang’ is ‘now the counsel is dependent’: ‘rǣd’ is ‘counsel, course of action, remedy’ (‘what is to be done’ in the idiomatic version) and ‘gelang’ ‘dependent on’, with ‘æt þē ānum’ ‘on you alone’ (‘ānum’ dative, ‘alone’); ‘eft’ is ‘again’. Hrothgar turns from the description to the request. ‘eft’, ‘again’, I take as looking back to the first rescue, when Beowulf freed Heorot of Grendel; that is my reading.

sentences.l: The land yet you do not know, the perilous place, where you may find the sinful man;
sentences.i: You do not yet know the land, that dangerous place where you may find the guilty creature;
sentences.n: ‘Eard’ is ‘land, dwelling-place’, accusative, placed first for emphasis; ‘gīt ne const’ is ‘you do not yet know’ (‘const’ the second person singular present of ‘cunnan’). ‘frēcne stōwe’ is ‘perilous place’, in apposition to ‘eard’. ‘ðǣr þū findan miht’ is ‘where you can find’. ‘sinnigne secg’ is ‘the sinful man’ (‘sinnig’, guilty, with ‘secg’, man, a word that can mean warrior); it is masculine, and I take it as Grendel’s mother, since the grammatical gender does not decide it. The manuscript has ‘fela sinnigne secg’; most editors cancel ‘fela’ (‘many’) as a slip and Holthausen thought a gap lay before it, with ‘fela’ the last word of the preceding line (apparatus). I follow the cancelling.

sentences.t: sēc gif þū dyrre!
sentences.l: seek, if you dare!
sentences.i: Seek it, if you dare!
sentences.n: ‘sēc’ is the imperative of ‘sēcan’, ‘seek’, and ‘gif þū dyrre’ is ‘if you dare’, ‘dyrre’ the subjunctive of ‘durran’, ‘dare’. The ‘if you dare’ clause turns the order into a challenge.

sentences.t:
Ic þē þā fǣhðe fēo lēanige,
ealdgestrēonum, swā ic ǣr dyde,
wundnum golde, gyf þū on weg cymest.’
sentences.l: I you for that feud with wealth will reward, with old-treasures, as I before did, with twisted gold, if you come away.’
sentences.i: I shall reward you for the feud with wealth, with ancient treasures, as I did before, with twisted gold, if you come away alive.’
sentences.n: ‘lēanige’ is the first person singular present of ‘lēanian’ with the sense of a future, ‘I will reward’; it takes the dative of the person (‘þē’) and the gift in the dative (‘fēo’, wealth). ‘þā fǣhðe’ is the accusative ‘for that feud’, what the reward is for. ‘ealdgestrēonum’ is ‘old treasures’ (‘eald’ + ‘gestrēon’), the stored hoard, ‘swā ic ǣr dyde’ ‘as I did before’ (the past of ‘dōn’), presumably the gifts after Grendel’s death. ‘wundnum golde’ is ‘with twisted (wrought) gold’: ‘wundnum’ is the dative of ‘wunden’, ‘twisted’. The manuscript is doubtful here, giving something like ‘wun/dini’ or ‘wun/dmi’; Grundtvig read ‘wunden-’, and Thorkelin, Holthausen and others ‘wundini’, so ‘wundnum’ is Klaeber’s reading and the end ‘num’ is italic. ‘on weg cymest’ is ‘come away’ (‘gyf’ a form of ‘gif’, if). The quotation mark closes Hrothgar’s speech.
